Learning Objectives
Outline nonsurgical treatment options for the management of knee osteoarthritis.
Review the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons evidence-based clinical practice
guidelines for appropriate nonsurgical management of knee osteoarthritis.

Learning Objectives
Knee osteoarthritis is a common cause of disability among adults in the United States.
Nonsurgical treatment options are available for the management of symptomatic knee

osteoarthritis. Goals include reducing pain, improving function and quality of life, and
delaying or potentially avoiding total knee arthroplasty.1 Comprehensive, evidence-
based guidelines have been established to assist surgeons in the appropriate use of
these modalities in patient care.2,3 Interim data on newer biologic treatment options
have yielded some promising results (Resources 1, 2, 3 and 4).
Nonsurgical Treatment Options and Guidelines
Rehabilitation, Education, and Wellness Activity
First line treatment for all patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis
Involves self-management programs and encourages physical activity consisting of
strengthening and low-impact aerobic exercises
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) recommendation: strong evidence in
support2

Rehabilitation, Education, and Wellness Activity
In addition to the overall physical and mental benefits, high- and low-intensity exercises
and strength training are beneficial in management of knee osteoarthritis. The
mechanism of pain relief likely is multifactorial in nature, involving mechanical and
physiologic factors, such as proprioceptive improvements and inflammatory modulation.
Treatment often is led by a healthcare practitioner, such as a physical therapist, and a
strong emphasis should be placed on patient education to promote healthy activities
and lifestyle changes.
Weight Loss
The risk of symptomatic knee osteoarthritis can be decreased by as much as 50% with weight
loss of as little as 5 kg in overweight individuals.1
Recommended for patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis and a body mass index greater
than 25 kg/m2,2
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
2/12

AAOS recommendation: Moderate evidence in support2

Weight Loss
Increased weight creates higher stress across the articular cartilage of the knee and may
contribute to increased pain and dysfunction. If combined with exercise, weight loss may
play a key role in improving pain and function. This likely is achieved via reduction in
compressive forces across the knee and via a modulation of inflammatory molecules (ie,
interleukin-6) in the joint. No optimal method for weight loss exists. Treatment plans
should be specific to the individual patient; however, many studies have shown that a
combination of diet and exercise is associated with better results.1
Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
Anti-inflammatory medications acting via selective and nonselective cyclooxygenase (COX)
inhibition, available commonly in oral and topical forms
Considered a first-line treatment for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis
Specific medication, route, dosing selection, and duration should be tailored based on patient
medical history and physician preference.
AAOS recommendation: Strong recommendation for the use of oral NSAIDs, with recognition
of the FDA black-box warning for concern of increased risk of serious cardiovascular
thrombotic events and serious gastrointenstinal events2

Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
NSAIDs (selective and nonselective COX inhibitors) have been endorsed as a first-line
nonsurgical treatment option for the management of symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis.2,3 These medications are commonly available via oral or topical routes
and should be tailored to the patient based on medical history and medication
accessibility. Concerns exist over the safety profiles of oral NSAIDs, particularly with
regard to the increased risks of gastrointestinal and renal adverse events. Selective COX-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Knee Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
3/12

2 inhibitors demonstrate a lower risk for gastrointestinal complications compared with
nonselective COX inhibitors but are associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular
complications.1 The lowest effective dose and duration of these medications should be
prescribed to minimize the potential for adverse events. Topical NSAIDs (ie, diclofenac
sodium 1% gel) have been shown to be an excellent alternative to oral NSAIDs in patients
with elevated risk profiles.1
Acetaminophen
Mechanism of action not completely understood; acts partially via central COX inhibition
without substantial anti-inflammatory effects
Commonly used as a first-line treatment option for the management of symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis
AAOS recommendation: Strong recommendation for the use of acetaminophen with
recognition of the FDA black-box warning for concern of overdose leading to hepatoxicity or
death2

Acetaminophen
Acetaminophen is a widely used pain reliever. This medication is commonly prescribed
as a first-line treatment option for the management of symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis.The 2021 AAOS clinical practice guideline reports high-quality evidence for
oral acetaminophen to be used to improve pain and function in the management of
knee osteoarthritis if not contraindicated.2 The available literature concludes that oral
acetaminophen compared with controls demonstrated a meaningful reduction in pain
and improved function, with no evidence of confounding heterogeneity. Overall,
acetaminophen is considered a safe medication with no evidence of substantially
increased adverse events among the included studies.2 The high frequency of the use of
acetaminophen in practice likely is attributable to its favorable gastrointestinal and renal
safety profile compared with NSAIDs. Regardless, safety concerns remain, particularly
with regard to the potential for hepatic toxicity at higher doses. Therefore,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
4/12

acetaminophen should be used conservatively, with dosing and duration not exceeding
recommendations (3,000 mg daily).
Tramadol
Analgesic medication acting as a partial opioid mu receptor agonist
AAOS recommendation: Strong evidence against the use of tramadol2

Tramadol
The most current high-quality studies consistently demonstrate that tramadol does not
effectively reduce pain or improve function in patients with symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis. Given the proven association between tramadol and adverse events
without clinical benefit, the 2021 AAOS clinical practice guideline reports strong evidence
against the use of tramadol in patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.2 In
addition, evidence links tramadol use to prolonged opioid use. Alternative treatment
options, such as oral NSAIDs and acetaminophen, are recommended for their relative
safety and effectiveness. In addition, avoidance of tramadol in nonsurgical treatment
may benefit patients who may progress to surgical treatment because its use has been
associated with adverse postoperative outcomes. 
Glucosamine and Chondroitin
Oral supplementation of compounds found in articular cartilage
Safe to use but limited effects compared with a placebo
AAOS recommendations: Limited recommendation for these oral supplements2

Glucosamine and Chondroitin
Glucosamine and chondroitin are natural constituents of native articular cartilage, and
oral supplementation of these compounds is thought to provide theoretic benefits in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Knee Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
5/12

patients with knee osteoarthritis via structure-modifying and anti-inflammatory effects
on articular structures. This evidence is inconsistent with studies reporting improvement
in pain and function or no change in patient outcomes for glucosamine and chondroitin;
however, none of the studies have demonstrated any harm to patients, leading to the
limited recommendation for glucosamine and chondroitin.
Mechanical Therapies and Physical Modalities
Mechanical and physical modalities available include corrective knee bracing, a lateral heel
wedge, acupuncture, manual manipulation or mobilization, physical agents, and
electrotherapeutic modalities.
AAOS recommendation
Knee bracing has a moderate recommendation for use in the management of knee
osteoarthritis.
Physical agents and electrotherapeutic modalities, including laser treatment, transcutaneous
electrical nerve stimulation, percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and extracorporeal
shockwave therapy, have a limited recommendation for use in the management of knee
osteoarthritis.
Manual therapy, massage, and acupuncture have a limited recommendation for use in the
management of knee osteoarthritis.
Lateral wedge insoles have a strong recommendation against their use in the management
of knee osteoarthritis.

Mechanical Therapies and Physical Modalities
Various mechanical therapies frequently are initiated early in the management of
symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, regardless whether at the instruction of healthcare
professionals. Common mechanical therapies, such as corrective valgus-directing knee
bracing and lateral heel wedges, are thought to redistribute load to the unaffected
compartment in patients with predominantly medial compartment osteoarthritis but
have shown moderate clinical efficacy in practice. The use of acupuncture has been
shown to provide inconsistent benefit, with concerns related to study designs; however,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Knee Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
6/12

no harm was identified in the studies on acupuncture, leading to the limited
recommendation in favor of acupuncture.
Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection
Strong anti-inflammatory medications with local effects because of direct delivery into the joint
Common in-office second-line treatment modality for the management of symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis
AAOS recommendation: Moderate recommendation for the use of intra-articular
corticosteroid injections2

Intra-Articular Corticosteroid Injection
Inflammation plays a key role in the symptomatology and progression of knee
osteoarthritis. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections have been shown to afford
effective symptomatic relief. Benefits over a placebo generally are short-lived, lasting
from several weeks to 6 months.1 The potential chondrotoxic effects of these
medications limit the frequency of use per year. Treatment response is variable, with
some evidence supporting the presence of an effusion and milder radiographic
osteoarthritis as predictors of longer pain relief.
Viscoelastic Supplementation
Injectable hyaluronan products available in various formulations
Hyaluronic acid is a key component of a healthy joint, adversely affected in patients with
osteoarthritis
AAOS recommendation: Moderate recommendation against the use of routine intra-articular
viscosupplementation injections2

Viscoelastic Supplementation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Knee Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
7/12

Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan that functions as a viscous
lubricant and an elastic shock absorber within the joint.1 The intra-articular
concentration of hyaluronic acid decreases as a result of the inflammatory osteoarthritis
cascade. Conflicting data with varying levels of evidence exist with regard to the efficacy
of viscoelastic supplementation, with some lower-level studies suggesting no difference
between hyaluronic acid injections and oral NSAIDs. These studies highlight the potential
utility of hyaluronic acid in patients who are unable to tolerate oral NSAIDs. More recent
higher-level studies, including level I meta-analyses, have failed to demonstrate
minimum clinically important functional improvements related to hyaluronic acid
injections. The AAOS clinical practice guideline recommends against its routine use but
recognizes it may have a role in select patients not deemed surgical candidates, such as
patients with early-stage arthritis or patients who cannot be medically optimized for
surgical treatment.2
Needle Lavage
Intra-articular saline irrigation with theoretic benefit of decreasing the concentration of
inflammatory mediators within the affected joint
Little or no benefit demonstrated with needle lavage in the management of knee osteoarthritis
AAOS recommendation: Moderate evidence against2
Platelet-Rich Plasma
Byproduct of autologous blood centrifugation yielding concentrated platelet samples
containing high levels of bioactive factors
AAOS recommendation: Limited recommendation for the use of intra-articular platelet-rich
plasma (PRP) injections2

Platelet-Rich Plasma
PRP contains high concentrations of growth factors and bioactive materials that
participate in the healing and inflammatory cascades.1 Despite some early evidence of
pain improvement in patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, the most recent
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:23 PM
AAOS | Nonsurgical Management of Knee Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000553
8/12

recommendations were inconsistent with regard to the use of PRP based on studies with
small cohorts. More recent data have shown promising short-term and long-term pain
and functional improvement compared with hyaluronic acid, particularly in younger
patients and those with lower severity of disease. A recent meta-analysis of 14
randomized controlled trials showed better long-term functional and pain-related
improvement in patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis who underwent PRP
treatment compared with hyaluronic acid treatment, with no considerable additional
risk.4 PRP is costly, and careful study of cost-effectiveness is advised. With the increasing
implementation of biologic treatment options in orthopaedics, new tools, such as the
AAOS biologics dashboard, have been designed to help orthopaedic surgeons navigate
the available data on biologic modalities and guide decision-making5 (Resources 5 and
6).
